notes.front: What is the `policyTypes` field of a NetworkPolicy?
notes.back: A list holding Ingress, Egress or both, saying which traffic directions the policy applies to for the Pods it selects.
notes.explanation: The field decides whether the policy governs traffic coming in to the selected Pods, traffic going out of them, or both.
notes.example: Like a door sign that says "entry", "exit" or both: the rules only cover the directions the sign names.
notes.evidence: Each NetworkPolicy includes a policyTypes list which may include either Ingress, Egress, or both. The policyTypes field indicates whether or not the given policy applies to ingress traffic to selected pod, egress traffic from selected pods, or both.
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, "Network Policies", "The NetworkPolicy resource"

notes.front: What does an `ipBlock` selector do in a NetworkPolicy rule?
notes.back: It selects IP CIDR ranges to allow as ingress sources or egress destinations.
notes.explanation: The other selectors pick Pods or namespaces by label; `ipBlock` picks addresses instead, for peers that labels cannot describe.
notes.example: Like allowing calls from a whole phone-number prefix rather than from named people in the company directory.
notes.evidence: ipBlock: This selects particular IP CIDR ranges to allow as ingress sources or egress destinations.
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, "Network Policies", "Behavior of to and from selectors"

notes.front: What does the `endPort` field let a NetworkPolicy rule do?
notes.back: Target a range of ports instead of a single port: from `port` up to `endPort`.
notes.explanation: Without it, each port in a rule is a single number; `endPort` turns the rule's `port` into the start of a range.
notes.example: Like a guest list that admits "rooms 200 to 250" instead of naming one room.
notes.evidence: When writing a NetworkPolicy, you can target a range of ports instead of a single port. This is achievable with the usage of the endPort field
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, "Network Policies", "Targeting a range of ports"

notes.front: If no NetworkPolicy exists in a namespace, what traffic may reach and leave its Pods?
notes.back: All ingress and all egress traffic is allowed.
notes.explanation: Isolation only begins when a policy selects a Pod, which is why the documentation offers default policies to change this behaviour.
notes.evidence: By default, if no policies exist in a namespace, then all ingress and egress traffic is allowed to and from pods in that namespace. The following examples let you change the default behavior in that namespace.
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, "Network Policies", "Default policies"

notes.front: In a NetworkPolicy, an empty `podSelector` (`{}`) selects {{c1::all Pods in the policy's namespace}}.
notes.back: All Pods in the policy's namespace.
notes.explanation: This is how every default policy reaches every Pod in the namespace without listing labels.
notes.evidence: An empty podSelector selects all pods in the namespace.
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, "Network Policies", "The NetworkPolicy resource"

notes.front: If a NetworkPolicy leaves out `policyTypes`, which types are set by default?
notes.back: Ingress always; Egress only if the policy has egress rules.
notes.explanation: So a policy written with only egress rules and no `policyTypes` also isolates ingress for the Pods it selects.
notes.evidence: If no policyTypes are specified on a NetworkPolicy then by default Ingress will always be set and Egress will be set if the NetworkPolicy has any egress rules.
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, "Network Policies", "The NetworkPolicy resource"

notes.front: What two things make up a default deny all ingress NetworkPolicy's `spec`?
notes.back: `podSelector: {}` and `policyTypes: [Ingress]`, with no ingress rules.
notes.explanation: The empty selector takes in every Pod in the namespace, and having no ingress rules means no incoming traffic is allowed to them.
notes.evidence: You can create a "default" ingress isolation policy for a namespace by creating a NetworkPolicy that selects all pods but does not allow any ingress traffic to those pods.
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, "Network Policies", "Default deny all ingress traffic"

notes.front: How do you build a default deny all egress NetworkPolicy for a namespace?
notes.back: Select all Pods (`podSelector: {}`), set `policyTypes: [Egress]`, and add no egress rules.
notes.explanation: Selecting every Pod while allowing no egress stops outgoing traffic even from Pods no other policy selects.
notes.evidence: You can create a "default" egress isolation policy for a namespace by creating a NetworkPolicy that selects all pods but does not allow any egress traffic from those pods.
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, "Network Policies", "Default deny all egress traffic"

notes.front: What common traffic does a default deny all egress policy also block?
notes.back: DNS traffic. Workloads that need name resolution need a separate policy allowing egress to the cluster's DNS service.
notes.explanation: Name lookups are themselves outgoing connections, so they fall under the egress deny like any other traffic.
notes.evidence: A default deny-all egress policy also blocks DNS traffic. If your workloads need DNS resolution, you must add a separate NetworkPolicy that allows egress to your cluster's DNS service.
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, "Network Policies", "Default deny all egress traffic"

notes.front: A NetworkPolicy with `podSelector: {}` and `policyTypes` listing {{c1::both Ingress and Egress}}, and no rules, denies all ingress and all egress in its namespace.
notes.back: Both Ingress and Egress.
notes.explanation: Naming both directions isolates every selected Pod both ways, and with no rules nothing is allowed either way.
notes.evidence: This ensures that even pods that aren't selected by any other NetworkPolicy will not be allowed ingress or egress traffic.
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, "Network Policies", "Default deny all ingress and all egress traffic"

notes.front: One `from` element holds both a `namespaceSelector` and a `podSelector`. Which peers does it allow?
notes.back: Only Pods matching the `podSelector` inside namespaces matching the `namespaceSelector` (both conditions together).
notes.explanation: Because the two selectors sit in the same list item, they combine into one peer description.
notes.evidence: namespaceSelector and podSelector: A single to/from entry that specifies both namespaceSelector and podSelector selects particular Pods within particular namespaces.
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, "Network Policies", "Behavior of to and from selectors"

notes.front: A `from` array has two elements: one `namespaceSelector` and, separately, one `podSelector`. Which peers does it allow?
notes.back: Either: matching Pods in the policy's own namespace, or any Pod in a matching namespace.
notes.explanation: Each element is its own allowed source, and a lone `podSelector` only looks in the policy's own namespace.
notes.evidence: It contains two elements in the from array, and allows connections from Pods in the local Namespace with the label role=client, or from any Pod in any namespace with the label user=alice.
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, "Network Policies", "Behavior of to and from selectors"

notes.front: What kind of IP addresses should an `ipBlock` name, and why?
notes.back: Cluster-external IP addresses, because Pod IP addresses are ephemeral and unpredictable.
notes.explanation: This is why other Pods are reached with Pod or namespace selectors rather than address ranges.
notes.evidence: These should be cluster-external IPs, since Pod IPs are ephemeral and unpredictable.
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, "Network Policies", "Behavior of to and from selectors"

notes.front: An ingress rule allows `ipBlock` `cidr: 172.17.0.0/16` with `except: [172.17.1.0/24]`. Which sources does it allow?
notes.back: Every address in 172.17.0.0/16 except those in 172.17.1.0/24.
notes.explanation: The `except` list carves smaller ranges out of the allowed CIDR, so one rule can allow a network while leaving out part of it.
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, "Network Policies", "The NetworkPolicy resource"

notes.front: Can a NetworkPolicy name a namespace directly, by its name?
notes.back: No. It must pick namespaces by their labels, using a `namespaceSelector`.
notes.explanation: The NetworkPolicy API has no namespace-name field, so a namespace is chosen through `matchLabels` or `matchExpressions`.
notes.evidence: It is not possible to directly specify the name of the namespaces in a NetworkPolicy. You must use a namespaceSelector with matchLabels or matchExpressions to select the namespaces based on their labels.
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, "Network Policies", "Targeting multiple namespaces by label"

notes.front: The control plane sets the immutable label {{c1::`kubernetes.io/metadata.name`}} on every namespace, with the namespace's name as its value.
notes.back: `kubernetes.io/metadata.name`
notes.explanation: Because the label always equals the name, a `namespaceSelector` on it targets one namespace by name.
notes.evidence: The Kubernetes control plane sets an immutable label kubernetes.io/metadata.name on all namespaces, the value of the label is the namespace name.
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, "Network Policies", "Targeting a Namespace by its name"

notes.front: What must be true of `endPort` compared with `port` in the same entry?
notes.back: `endPort` must be equal to or greater than `port`.
notes.explanation: The pair describes a range that starts at `port` and ends at `endPort`.
notes.evidence: The endPort field must be equal to or greater than the port field.
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, "Network Policies", "Targeting a range of ports"

notes.front: Can you set `endPort` on its own, and can it be a named port?
notes.back: No to both: `endPort` needs `port` to be set too, and both must be numeric.
notes.explanation: These are two of the restrictions the documentation lists for the field.
notes.evidence: endPort can only be defined if port is also defined. Both ports must be numeric.
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, "Network Policies", "Targeting a range of ports"

notes.front: In the most common network plugin implementation, how is traffic to and from `hostNetwork` Pods treated by NetworkPolicy?
notes.back: The same as all other traffic to and from the node's IP address; selectors ignore those Pods.
notes.explanation: The documentation calls this behaviour undefined but says this treatment is the most common implementation.
notes.evidence: The network plugin cannot properly distinguish hostNetwork pod traffic, and so it ignores hostNetwork pods when matching podSelector and namespaceSelector. Traffic to/from hostNetwork pods is treated the same as all other traffic to/from the node IP. (This is the most common implementation.)
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, "Network Policies", "NetworkPolicy and hostNetwork pods"

notes.front: How can a NetworkPolicy allow traffic from a `hostNetwork` Pod?
notes.back: With an `ipBlock` rule, since the Pod shares its node's IP address and its connections count as node connections.
notes.explanation: A Pod selector may not match such a Pod, but its address is the node's, which an address range can name.
notes.evidence: since hostNetwork pods have the same IP addresses as the nodes they reside on, their connections will be treated as node connections. For example, you can allow traffic from a hostNetwork Pod using an ipBlock rule.
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, "Network Policies", "NetworkPolicy and hostNetwork pods"

notes.front: You need TLS between services. Can the NetworkPolicy API do it, and if not, what does the documentation suggest?
notes.back: No. Use a service mesh or an ingress controller.
notes.explanation: The documentation lists "anything TLS related" among the things the API cannot do, at least not yet.
notes.evidence: Anything TLS related (use a service mesh or ingress controller for this).
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, "Network Policies", "What you can't do with network policies (at least, not yet)"

notes.front: Can a NetworkPolicy contain an explicit deny rule?
notes.back: No. The model is deny by default, with only allow rules added.
notes.explanation: To block something, you isolate the Pod and then allow only what it needs.
notes.evidence: The ability to explicitly deny policies (currently the model for NetworkPolicies are deny by default, with only the ability to add allow rules).
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, "Network Policies", "What you can't do with network policies (at least, not yet)"

notes.front: Can a NetworkPolicy target a Service by its name? What is the usual workaround?
notes.back: No. Target the Pods or namespaces behind it by their labels instead.
notes.explanation: The documentation calls label targeting "often a viable workaround" for the missing Service-name targeting.
notes.evidence: Targeting of services by name (you can, however, target pods or namespaces by their labels, which is often a viable workaround).
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, "Network Policies", "What you can't do with network policies (at least, not yet)"

notes.front: What host access does kube-bench need when run inside a Pod?
notes.back: The host's process namespace, to check running processes, and host directories holding config and other files.
notes.explanation: The kube-bench documentation says the process namespace is needed to check the running processes, and the host directories for the config files stored there.
notes.evidence: You can run kube-bench inside a pod, but it will need access to the host's PID namespace in order to check the running processes, as well as access to some directories on the host where config files and other files are stored.
notes.source: kube-bench README, "Running kube-bench"

notes.front: You ran kube-bench with its supplied `job.yaml`. Where do you read the results?
notes.back: In the Job's Pod logs, for example with `kubectl logs <pod>`.
notes.explanation: In the kube-bench example the Job Pod reaches Completed and the report is then read from its logs.
notes.evidence: The results are held in the pod's logs
notes.source: kube-bench README, "Running kube-bench"

notes.front: By default, how does kube-bench choose which set of CIS Benchmark tests to run?
notes.back: From the Kubernetes version running on the machine.
notes.explanation: The kube-bench documentation says this is the default, so you do not normally pick the benchmark version yourself.
notes.evidence: By default, kube-bench will determine the test set to run based on the Kubernetes version running on the machine.
notes.source: kube-bench README, "Please Note"

notes.front: You edit a manifest in the kubelet's static Pod directory (for example `/etc/kubernetes/manifests`). Do you need to apply it with `kubectl`?
notes.back: No. The kubelet scans the directory periodically and creates or deletes static Pods as files appear or disappear.
notes.explanation: Changes appear as the kubelet rescans the directory, so fixing a static Pod means editing its file on the node.
notes.evidence: which periodically scans the directory and creates/deletes static Pods as YAML/JSON files appear/disappear there.
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, "Create static Pods", "Filesystem-hosted static Pod manifest"

notes.front: Before editing `kube-apiserver.yaml` you copy it to `kube-apiserver.yaml.backup` in the same directory. What goes wrong?
notes.back: The kubelet reads both files and tries to create a static Pod from each. Store backups outside the directory.
notes.explanation: The kubelet does not filter by file extension, and with two same-named Pods the outdated backup can silently take effect.
notes.evidence: if you create a backup of a manifest by running cp kube-apiserver.yaml kube-apiserver.yaml.backup , the kubelet will read both files and attempt to create a static Pod from each.
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, "Create static Pods", "Filesystem-hosted static Pod manifest"

notes.front: You want only Pods labelled `app=scraper` in namespaces labelled `team=ops` to reach a database. Which `from` shape does that?
notes.choices:
A) One element holding both `namespaceSelector: {team: ops}` and `podSelector: {app: scraper}`
B) Two elements: `- namespaceSelector: {team: ops}` and `- podSelector: {app: scraper}`
C) One element with only `podSelector: {app: scraper}`
D) One `ipBlock` covering the ops nodes
notes.back: A) One element holding both selectors, so both conditions must match.
notes.explanation: Selectors inside a single `from` entry select particular Pods within particular namespaces.
notes.choicesExplained: B allows any Pod in ops namespaces, or scraper Pods in the local namespace. C only looks in the policy's own namespace. D names addresses, and Pod addresses are unpredictable.
notes.evidence: namespaceSelector and podSelector: A single to/from entry that specifies both namespaceSelector and podSelector selects particular Pods within particular namespaces.
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, "Network Policies", "Behavior of to and from selectors"

notes.front: After you apply a default deny all egress policy in namespace `shop`, its Pods can no longer resolve any hostnames. What is the fix that keeps the deny in place?
notes.choices:
A) Delete the deny policy
B) Add a separate NetworkPolicy allowing egress to the cluster's DNS service
C) Add Ingress to the deny policy's `policyTypes`
D) Restart the Pods
notes.back: B) Add a separate policy that allows egress to the cluster's DNS service.
notes.explanation: The deny also blocks DNS traffic, and allow rules from another policy add back only what is needed.
notes.choicesExplained: A removes the protection altogether. C adds ingress isolation and blocks even more. D changes nothing, as the policy still selects the new Pods.
notes.evidence: A default deny-all egress policy also blocks DNS traffic. If your workloads need DNS resolution, you must add a separate NetworkPolicy that allows egress to your cluster's DNS service.
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, "Network Policies", "Default deny all egress traffic"

notes.front: A new namespace `vault` must start with no traffic in or out of any Pod until allow rules are added. Which policy do you apply?
notes.choices:
A) `podSelector: {}` with `policyTypes: [Ingress]` and no rules
B) `podSelector: {}` with `policyTypes: [Ingress, Egress]` and no rules
C) `podSelector: {}` with an ingress rule `from: [{}]`
D) No policy at all
notes.back: B) Select all Pods, list both Ingress and Egress, and add no rules.
notes.explanation: That is the documented default deny all ingress and all egress policy.
notes.choicesExplained: A leaves egress untouched. C allows all ingress rather than denying it. D leaves all traffic allowed, which is the default with no policies.
notes.evidence: You can create a "default" policy for a namespace which prevents all ingress AND egress traffic by creating the following NetworkPolicy in that namespace.
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, "Network Policies", "Default deny all ingress and all egress traffic"

notes.front: An egress rule must allow traffic to the namespace called `payments`, which has no custom labels. What do you write in the `to` entry?
notes.choices:
A) `namespace: payments`
B) `namespaceSelector: {matchLabels: {kubernetes.io/metadata.name: payments}}`
C) `podSelector: {matchLabels: {namespace: payments}}`
D) You must first add a custom label to the namespace
notes.back: B) A `namespaceSelector` on the label `kubernetes.io/metadata.name: payments`.
notes.explanation: The control plane sets that immutable label on every namespace, so it can stand in for the name.
notes.choicesExplained: A is not a NetworkPolicy field. C looks for a Pod label in the policy's own namespace. D is unnecessary, as the name label already exists.
notes.evidence: While NetworkPolicy cannot target a namespace by its name with some object field, you can use the standardized label to target a specific namespace.
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, "Network Policies", "Targeting a Namespace by its name"

notes.front: kube-bench flags a kube-apiserver command-line setting on a kubeadm control plane node. Where do you make the fix?
notes.choices:
A) `kubectl edit pod kube-apiserver-<node> -n kube-system`
B) Edit `/etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-apiserver.yaml` on that node
C) Save a copy as `kube-apiserver.yaml.new` in the same directory
D) Delete the kube-apiserver mirror Pod with `kubectl delete`
notes.back: B) Edit the static Pod manifest on the node; the kubelet picks up the change.
notes.explanation: The kubelet watches that directory and recreates static Pods as their files change.
notes.choicesExplained: A edits the mirror Pod, not the file the kubelet runs. C leaves two manifests for the kubelet to read. D does not remove or change the static Pod; the kubelet keeps it running.
notes.evidence: The running kubelet periodically scans the configured directory ( /etc/kubernetes/manifests in our example) for changes and adds/removes Pods as files appear/disappear in this directory.
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, "Create static Pods", "Dynamic addition and removal of static pods"

notes.front: Default deny all ingress versus default deny all ingress and egress: what is the only difference in their specs?
notes.back: `policyTypes`: the first lists only Ingress; the second lists Ingress and Egress.
notes.explanation: Both select every Pod with an empty `podSelector` and allow nothing; `policyTypes` decides which directions are isolated.
notes.evidence: The policyTypes field indicates whether or not the given policy applies to ingress traffic to selected pod, egress traffic from selected pods, or both.
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, "Network Policies", "The NetworkPolicy resource"
